live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient with diabetes is unconscious and has a very low capillary glucose.

What is the priority?

options.A: Give buccal glucose gel and wait for the patient to wake up
options.B: Give a sugary drink with the patient sitting upright
options.C: Support the airway and treat with IV glucose or IM glucagon
options.D: Send a laboratory glucose and treat once confirmed
options.E: Give the usual insulin dose and recheck glucose in one hour

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Support the airway and treat with IV glucose or IM glucagon
live_plab_copy.why_correct: An unconscious hypoglycaemic patient needs ABC support and urgent parenteral treatment with IV glucose (e.g. 10% glucose) or IM glucagon, because oral treatment is unsafe (JBDS Hospital management of hypoglycaemia).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Buccal glucose gel is not recommended in an unconscious patient because of aspiration risk and unreliable absorption. B. An unconscious patient cannot swallow safely, so oral drinks risk aspiration. D. Waiting for a laboratory result delays urgent treatment and risks brain injury. E. Insulin would worsen life-threatening hypoglycaemia.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Hypoglycaemia with unconsciousness needs parenteral treatment: support the airway and give IV glucose or IM glucagon, because nothing should be given by mouth to a patient who cannot swallow safely.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Patient with diabetes ↓ Unconscious ↓ Very low capillary glucose ↓ Oral treatment unsafe ↓ Airway support with IV glucose or IM glucagon
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, buccal glucose gel — it seems gentle and quick, but it is not recommended in an unconscious patient because of aspiration risk and unreliable absorption.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Unconscious hypoglycaemia: protect the airway and give IV glucose or IM glucagon.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with acromegaly develops headaches and loss of peripheral vision. What complication should be suspected?

options.A: Optic chiasm compression
options.B: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
options.C: Bilateral age-related cataract
options.D: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
options.E: Demyelinating optic neuritis

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Optic chiasm compression
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A pituitary macroadenoma can compress the optic chiasm and cause bitemporal visual-field loss.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes painful red eye and visual disturbance. C. Cataract causes gradual visual blurring. D. Retinal detachment causes a field defect or visual phenomena from retinal separation. E. Optic neuritis commonly causes painful visual loss rather than the classic field defect from a pituitary mass.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A pituitary macroadenoma, such as in acromegaly, can press on the optic chiasm and cause bitemporal hemianopia; formal visual field testing is part of assessment.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Acromegaly means a pituitary adenoma ↓ Headache suggests a mass effect ↓ Loss of peripheral vision ↓ Chiasm sits just above the pituitary ↓ Optic chiasm compression
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, demyelinating optic neuritis — it also causes visual loss, but usually painful central loss in one eye, not peripheral field loss from a pituitary mass.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Pituitary tumour with peripheral visual loss: think chiasmal compression.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with diabetes develops vomiting and is unable to maintain their normal food and fluid intake. What is an important principle of sick-day management?

options.A: Stop insulin and tablets until eating and drinking normally
options.B: Reduce fluid intake to limit vomiting and avoid fluid overload
options.C: Continue usual doses and check capillary glucose once each morning
options.D: Omit basal insulin until the vomiting has stopped completely
options.E: Seek advice promptly and monitor glucose more frequently

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Seek advice promptly and monitor glucose more frequently
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Acute illness can destabilise diabetes control and increase the risk of metabolic emergencies, so closer monitoring and appropriate sick-day advice are important.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Insulin should not be stopped during illness as this risks DKA; only some tablets may need to be withheld. B. Fluid intake should be maintained to avoid dehydration; fluid overload is not the concern. C. Monitoring should be increased during illness, not kept to a single daily check. D. Basal insulin should be continued; omitting it risks ketoacidosis.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Sick-day rules: never stop insulin, monitor glucose (and ketones in type 1) more often, keep drinking, and seek advice early; some tablets, such as metformin, may need pausing.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Diabetes ↓ Vomiting and reduced intake ↓ Illness raises insulin needs and dehydration risk ↓ Risk of metabolic emergency ↓ Seek advice promptly and monitor glucose more frequently
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, stopping insulin and tablets — seems logical when not eating, but stopping insulin risks DKA; insulin continues, and only some tablets may need pausing.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Illness with diabetes: never stop insulin; monitor more and seek advice.

A patient with known primary adrenal insufficiency develops vomiting, abdominal pain, hypotension and severe weakness during an acute infection.

What is the most important diagnosis?

options.A: Phaeochromocytoma
options.B: Primary hyperparathyroidism
options.C: Cushing syndrome
options.D: Addisonian crisis
options.E: Hyperthyroidism

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Addisonian crisis
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Acute illness can precipitate adrenal crisis, causing hypotension, vomiting, abdominal pain and profound weakness in someone with adrenal insufficiency.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic catecholamine excess and hypertension. B. Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia rather than acute circulatory collapse. C. Cushing syndrome results from excess cortisol rather than deficiency. E. Hyperthyroidism causes symptoms such as weight loss, tremor and palpitations.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Adrenal crisis: give IM or IV hydrocortisone immediately with IV fluids, without waiting for results; patients need sick-day rules and an emergency injection kit.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Known primary adrenal insufficiency ↓ Acute infection raises steroid requirement ↓ Vomiting, abdominal pain, hypotension, weakness ↓ Acute cortisol deficiency ↓ Addisonian crisis
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, phaeochromocytoma — causes dramatic episodes with abdominal pain, but it produces hypertension, not hypotension and collapse.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Known Addison's plus illness, vomiting and hypotension: adrenal crisis, give hydrocortisone now.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Bone pain and proximal weakness with low sun exposure suggest vitamin D deficiency.

live_plab_copy.stem: Which clinical feature is particularly suggestive of Cushing syndrome?

options.A: Marked weight loss with hyperpigmentation only
options.B: Recurrent hypoglycaemia
options.C: Proximal muscle weakness
options.D: Persistent hypothermia
options.E: Severe bradycardia

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Proximal muscle weakness
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Excess cortisol can cause proximal muscle weakness, alongside features such as central weight gain, hypertension and skin changes.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Weight loss and hyperpigmentation suggest other conditions, particularly adrenal insufficiency. B. Cushing syndrome is associated with hyperglycaemia rather than recurrent hypoglycaemia. D. Hypothermia is not characteristic. E. Bradycardia is not characteristic.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Proximal myopathy, easy bruising, wide purple striae and thin skin are among the most discriminating features of Cushing syndrome; exogenous steroids are the commonest cause.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Features of Cushing syndrome ↓ Excess cortisol ↓ Protein breakdown in skeletal muscle ↓ Proximal muscle weakness
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, weight loss with hyperpigmentation — pigmentation can occur in ACTH-driven Cushing's, which tempts, but weight loss with pigmentation points to adrenal insufficiency.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Proximal weakness, bruising and striae suggest Cushing syndrome.

A patient has weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor and palpitations.

Which thyroid function pattern is most consistent with primary hyperthyroidism?

options.A: High TSH with low free T4
options.B: High TSH with low free T3
options.C: Low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3
options.D: High TSH with high free T4 as the usual pattern
options.E: Normal thyroid function tests in every case

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. High TSH with low free T4 indicates primary hypothyroidism. B. High TSH with low free T3 is a hypothyroid pattern. D. High TSH with high free T4 suggests rare causes such as a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, not primary hyperthyroidism. E. Clinical hyperthyroidism is accompanied by abnormal thyroid function tests.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In primary hyperthyroidism excess thyroid hormone suppresses TSH, giving a low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3; T3 toxicosis may show a raised T3 only.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations ↓ Clinical hyperthyroidism ↓ Excess hormone suppresses pituitary TSH ↓ Low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, high TSH with high free T4 — high hormone levels seem to fit, but a high TSH alongside them suggests a rare TSH-secreting adenoma, not primary hyperthyroidism.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Primary hyperthyroidism: low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3.

A 33-year-old woman has fatigue, weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations and a fine tremor.

Which investigation is most appropriate initially?

options.A: Thyroid-stimulating hormone
options.B: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies
options.C: Plasma metanephrines
options.D: Radioisotope thyroid uptake scan
options.E: Serum adjusted calcium

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Thyroid-stimulating hormone
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Thyroid function testing, beginning with TSH in most initial assessments, is appropriate when hyperthyroidism is suspected.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. TPO antibodies do not establish thyroid status and are not the first test. C. Metanephrines are measured for suspected phaeochromocytoma, which is far less likely than thyrotoxicosis; thyroid function should be checked first. D. Isotope uptake scanning helps determine the cause after hyperthyroidism is confirmed biochemically. E. Calcium does not assess thyroid function.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In suspected hyperthyroidism, a suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and/or T3 confirms thyrotoxicosis; antibodies or uptake scanning then define the cause.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Weight loss and heat intolerance ↓ Palpitations and fine tremor ↓ Suspected thyrotoxicosis ↓ Check TSH first
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, radioisotope thyroid uptake scan — it is used in hyperthyroidism, but only to find the cause after biochemical confirmation.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Suspected thyroid disease: confirm with TSH first, find the cause later.

A 33-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight loss, diarrhoea and tremor. Her pulse is 115 beats/minute and she is visibly anxious.

Which diagnosis should be considered?

options.A: Iron-deficiency anaemia only
options.B: Hyperthyroidism
options.C: Addison disease
options.D: Hypothyroidism
options.E: Hypoparathyroidism

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Hyperthyroidism
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Weight loss, diarrhoea, tremor, anxiety and tachycardia are typical features of excess thyroid hormone.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Anaemia can cause fatigue and tachycardia but does not explain the whole symptom pattern. C. Addison disease commonly causes weight loss and hypotension but not this hypermetabolic pattern. D. Hypothyroidism more commonly causes weight gain, constipation and bradycardia. E. Hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcaemia-related symptoms.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Check TSH first: in hyperthyroidism it is suppressed with raised free T4 or T3; Graves disease is the commonest cause, and beta-blockers ease adrenergic symptoms while definitive treatment is planned.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Young woman ↓ Weight loss and diarrhoea ↓ Tremor and anxiety ↓ Tachycardia at 115 beats/minute ↓ Hyperthyroidism
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, hypothyroidism — the other thyroid option, but it causes weight gain, constipation and bradycardia, the opposite of this hypermetabolic picture.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Weight loss, tremor, diarrhoea and tachycardia point to hyperthyroidism.

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Relatives cannot override or consent on behalf of an adult with capacity. C. Best-interests decisions apply only when a person lacks capacity. D. A court cannot authorise treatment against the valid refusal of an adult with capacity. E. An unwise decision is not in itself evidence of a lack of capacity.
live_plab_copy.pearl: An adult with capacity may refuse treatment after adequate information, even if the decision seems unwise; the refusal must be respected and neither relatives nor best interests can override it.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Competent adult ↓ Adequate information given ↓ Refuses the procedure ↓ Capacity means the right to refuse ↓ Respect the refusal
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, reassessing capacity because the decision seems unwise — it tempts as caution, but an unwise decision is not in itself evidence that capacity is lacking.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A valid refusal from an adult with capacity must be respected, however unwise it seems.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient with a learning disability refuses a particular investigation.

What is the correct approach?

options.A: Assess capacity for this specific decision
options.B: Proceed in their best interests because of the disability
options.C: Ask the next of kin to give consent instead
options.D: Defer the investigation indefinitely
options.E: Accept the refusal without exploring it further

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Assess capacity for this specific decision
live_plab_copy.why_correct: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 requires capacity to be presumed and assessed for each specific decision; a learning disability does not by itself mean a person lacks capacity, and they should be supported to decide (e.g. with easy-read information).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Best-interests decisions apply only after capacity has been assessed and found lacking, not because of a diagnosis. C. Families cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a relevant lasting power of attorney and the person lacks capacity. D. Indefinite deferral avoids supporting the patient to make an informed decision. E. The patient should be supported to understand the decision and capacity assessed, rather than the refusal being accepted without exploration.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Capacity is presumed and assessed for each specific decision at the time it is needed; a learning disability does not by itself mean a person lacks capacity, and they should be supported to decide.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Learning disability ↓ Refuses a specific investigation ↓ Capacity is decision-specific and presumed ↓ Diagnosis alone does not remove capacity ↓ Assess capacity for this decision
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, proceeding in their best interests — it sounds protective, but best interests apply only once capacity is assessed and found lacking, never because of a diagnosis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A diagnosis never removes capacity; assess it for the specific decision and support the person.
